short: Sattva, rajas and tamas — the three strands of all nature.
beginner: The gunas are three basic qualities that make up everything in nature: sattva (clarity, balance), rajas (activity, passion) and tamas (inertia, dullness). Their shifting mix explains differences in things, moods and people.
what: Guna means 'strand' or 'quality'. In Sankhya the three gunas are the constituents of prakriti; when they are in balance nature is unmanifest, and their disturbance produces the world. The Gita uses the gunas extensively — in chapter 14 to explain bondage, and in chapters 17–18 to classify faith, food, action, knowledge, intellect and happiness. Rising beyond all three is the goal. In Nyaya-Vaisheshika, by contrast, guna is a technical term for 'quality' as a category.
scholar: Sankhya Karika 12–13 describes the gunas' natures and interdependence. The Gita's 'gunatita' (one who has gone beyond the gunas) of 14.22–26 is a key ideal. The Vaisheshika use of guna (24 qualities such as colour, taste, number) is a different, unrelated technical sense and should not be confused with the triguna.

perspectives.view: The three gunas are the actual constituents of prakriti, always together in varying proportions; the world is their transformation.
The seen consists of the gunas; the yogi aims at a sattvic mind clear enough to discern the seer, and finally beyond the gunas altogether.
The Vedanta schools adopt the gunas to describe prakriti or maya, while locating the Self or God beyond them.
Guna here means 'quality' as one of the basic categories of reality — a different technical sense from the three strands.

follow.note: The gunas as the constituents of nature.
Actions are done by the gunas; the ego thinks 'I am the doer'.
Sattva, rajas and tamas bind the embodied soul.
Faith is of three kinds, according to one's nature.
The larger Sankhya map in which the gunas operate.
